title: Why Your Phone Gets Warm
title_zh: 为什么你的手机会发热
author: Emily Carter
summary: Phones get warm because their batteries and chips turn some energy into heat, and a few simple habits can keep them cool and healthy.
paragraphs: Have you ever picked up your phone and felt that it was warm? This is very common. Most of the time, it is not a problem. A phone is a small computer, and every computer makes some heat when it works. The harder it works, the warmer it gets.

Inside your phone there is a battery and a main chip. The chip is the brain of the phone. When you play a game, watch a video, or use the camera, the chip does a lot of work very quickly. Some of the energy from the battery becomes heat instead of useful work.

Charging also makes a phone warm. When electricity goes into the battery, the battery gets a little hot. Fast chargers send more power in a short time, so the phone can feel warmer than usual. This is normal, and modern phones are made to handle it.

The weather is important too. If you leave your phone in the sun or in a hot car, it can get very hot. Phones do not like high heat. Some phones will show a message and stop working for a while until they cool down.

Your phone also works hard when the signal is weak. In a train, a basement, or a small village far from a tower, the phone uses more power to stay connected. It searches again and again for a better signal. This makes the battery work harder, and the phone slowly becomes warm in your pocket.

Many phones today can protect themselves. When they get too warm, they make the screen a little darker. They may also slow down the chip or stop fast charging for a while. You might notice that a game feels slower than usual. This is the phone trying to cool itself down safely.

Heat is not good for batteries over a long time. A battery that often gets hot will lose its power faster. After a year or two, it may not last a full day. That is why it is smart to keep your phone cool when you can.

Here are some easy tips. Take off a thick case when you charge your phone. Do not play big games while the phone is charging. Close apps that you are not using. Keep the phone out of direct sunlight, and never put it under your pillow at night.

If your phone becomes very hot when you are not using it, something may be wrong. An app may be running in the background, or the battery may be old. In that case, restart the phone. If the problem does not stop, ask a repair shop for help.

title: Opening a Small Coffee Shop
title_zh: 开一家小咖啡店
author: Daniel Brooks
summary: Many people dream of opening a coffee shop, but success depends on careful planning, a good location, and friendly service every day.
paragraphs: Many people dream of opening their own coffee shop. They imagine the smell of fresh coffee, happy customers, and music playing softly. It is a nice dream, but running a small shop is also hard work. Before you open the door, you need a clear plan.

The first question is money. You need money for rent, machines, cups, coffee beans, and workers. A good coffee machine can cost a lot. Most new owners use their savings or borrow money from a bank. It is wise to keep some extra money for the first few months.

Location is very important. A shop near a busy street, a school, or an office building will see more people walking by. But rent in these places is often high. Some owners choose a quiet street with lower rent and work hard to make the shop famous.

Next, think about what makes your shop special. There are many coffee shops in most cities. Maybe you sell homemade cakes. Maybe your shop has big windows and comfortable chairs for reading. Maybe you know the name of every regular customer. Small things like these bring people back.

Prices need careful thought. If your coffee is too cheap, you will not make enough money. If it is too expensive, people will go somewhere else. Many owners look at other shops nearby and then choose a price that feels fair for the quality they offer.

Good workers can make or break a small shop. A friendly barista who smiles and remembers orders is worth a lot. Owners need to train new workers well, pay them fairly, and treat them with respect. When workers are happy, customers can feel it, and they are more likely to return.

Today, the internet also matters. Many people look at photos and reviews online before they visit a new place. A simple website, a map listing, and a few nice pictures on social media can help. Some shops also offer delivery through apps, so people can enjoy their coffee at home or at work.

The work starts early. Many coffee shop owners wake up before six o'clock every morning. They clean, prepare food, check supplies, and serve customers all day. On some days, few people come in. On other days, there is a long line at the door.

Is it worth it? For many owners, the answer is yes. They enjoy meeting people and building something of their own. A small coffee shop can become a warm place in the neighborhood, where friends meet and new ideas begin over a simple cup.

title: A Short History of Tea Around the World
title_zh: 茶在世界各地的简史
author: Lin Mei
summary: Tea began in China thousands of years ago and slowly traveled across the world, where each country made its own tea traditions.
paragraphs: Tea is one of the most popular drinks in the world. Every day, millions of people start their morning with a hot cup. But where did tea come from, and how did it become so loved in so many different countries? The story goes back thousands of years.

Most historians agree that tea began in China. An old story says that a leaf fell into a pot of hot water, and the emperor liked the taste. Nobody knows if this story is true, but people in China were drinking tea a very long time ago.

At first, tea was used as a kind of medicine. Later, it became a daily drink. Tea houses opened in towns and cities, and people met there to talk, read, and rest. Writers wrote poems about tea, and some people spent their whole lives learning how to make it well.

Tea then traveled to Japan and Korea. In Japan, people created a special tea ceremony. In this ceremony, every move is slow and careful. The host makes green tea for the guests, and everyone enjoys a quiet, peaceful moment together.

Traders carried tea to Europe about four hundred years ago. In Britain, tea became very popular. People added milk and sugar, and afternoon tea with small cakes became a famous custom. Today, many British people still drink several cups of tea every day.

Other countries also have their own tea habits. In Morocco, people drink sweet green tea with fresh mint. In India, chai is made with milk and spices. In Russia, families once used a large metal pot to keep water hot for tea all day long.

In some places, tea is not only a drink but also a part of daily meals. In Tibet, people make butter tea with salt. It is warm and rich, and it gives energy in the cold mountains. In parts of Southeast Asia, people even eat tea leaves in salads with nuts and beans.

How is tea made? Most tea comes from the same plant. Farmers pick young green leaves by hand. Then the leaves are dried, rolled, or heated in different ways. Green tea is heated soon after picking. Black tea is left in the air for longer, so it becomes dark and strong.

Today, you can find tea almost everywhere. There is black tea, green tea, white tea, and many more. Some people like it hot, and some like it cold with ice. Wherever you go, a cup of tea is often a sign of welcome and friendship.

title: Simple Ways to Sleep Better
title_zh: 改善睡眠的简单方法
author: Sarah Collins
summary: Good sleep helps the body and mind, and small changes to daily habits can make it easier to fall asleep and wake up rested.
paragraphs: Sleep is very important for our health. When we sleep well, we feel happy and full of energy. When we sleep badly, it is hard to think, work, or study. Many people do not get enough sleep. The good news is that a few small changes can help a lot.

First, try to go to bed at the same time every night. Also try to wake up at the same time every morning, even on weekends. Your body has a clock inside it. When you follow a regular plan, this clock works better, and sleep comes more easily.

Second, be careful with screens. Phones, tablets, and computers give off a bright light. This light tells your brain that it is still daytime. Try to put your phone away about one hour before bed. You can read a paper book or listen to quiet music instead.

Third, think about what you eat and drink. Coffee and strong tea can keep you awake for many hours. It is better not to drink them in the afternoon or evening. A big dinner late at night can also make sleep difficult, so try to eat earlier.

Your bedroom matters too. A good bedroom for sleep is dark, quiet, and a little cool. If there is noise outside, you can use soft earplugs. Thick curtains can block light from the street. A comfortable bed and pillow also make a big difference.

Short naps can be good, but long naps can cause trouble. If you sleep for two hours in the afternoon, you may not feel tired at bedtime. A nap of twenty or thirty minutes is usually enough to feel fresh. Try to take it before three o'clock in the afternoon.

It can also help to have a calm routine before bed. You might take a warm shower, drink a glass of warm milk, or write a few lines in a notebook. Doing the same things every night tells your body that it is time to rest and get ready for sleep.

Exercise is another helpful habit. People who walk, run, or play sports during the day often sleep better at night. But do not do hard exercise just before bed, because it can wake your body up. A short walk after dinner is a nice idea.

Finally, do not worry too much if you cannot sleep. Lying in bed and feeling stressed only makes it worse. Get up, sit in another room, and do something calm. When you feel tired again, go back to bed. With time and patience, better sleep will come.

title: How Recommendation Algorithms Choose Your Next Video
title_zh: 推荐算法如何选择你的下一个视频
author: Marcus Reed
summary: Video platforms use recommendation systems that learn from your behavior, which makes watching easy but also raises questions about choice and variety.
paragraphs: If you have ever opened a video app to watch one short clip and looked up an hour later, you have experienced the power of a recommendation algorithm. These systems decide which videos appear on your screen, and they are among the most influential pieces of software in the world today.

At a basic level, a recommendation system tries to predict what you will enjoy. It collects information about your behavior: which videos you click, how long you watch, what you skip, and what you like or share. Every action becomes a signal that helps the system understand your interests.

One common method is called collaborative filtering. The idea is simple. If you and another person both enjoyed the same ten videos, you will probably enjoy other videos that person liked. By comparing millions of users, the system can find patterns that no human could notice.

Another method looks at the content itself. The system studies titles, descriptions, images, and even the sound in each video. If you often watch cooking videos about Italian food, it will suggest more videos with similar features, even if they are brand new and few people have seen them.

Most modern platforms combine these approaches and use machine learning to improve over time. Their main goal is usually to keep you watching. Watch time is easy to measure, and it is closely connected to advertising income, which is how many free platforms earn money.

Timing and context also play a role. Many systems consider the hour of the day, the type of device, and even your location. Someone browsing on a phone during a morning commute may receive shorter clips, while the same person relaxing on a television in the evening might be offered longer documentaries or full episodes.

Creators pay close attention to these rules, even though platforms rarely explain them in detail. They experiment with eye-catching thumbnails, dramatic titles, and strong openings, because the first few seconds often decide whether viewers keep watching. As a result, the algorithm shapes not only what we see but also how videos are made.

This design has clear benefits. Viewers discover creators they would never find on their own, and small channels can suddenly reach a huge audience. However, critics worry that algorithms can trap people in a bubble, showing them only the same type of content and opinions again and again.

There are ways to take back some control. You can clear your watch history, tell the app that you are not interested in certain videos, or search for topics directly instead of relying on the home page. Understanding how the system works is the first step toward using it wisely.

title: Why Companies Are Trying the Four-Day Week
title_zh: 为什么企业开始尝试四天工作制
author: Rachel Kim
summary: A growing number of companies are testing a four-day working week, and early results suggest that productivity can stay high while workers feel healthier.
paragraphs: For most of the last century, the five-day working week has been the standard in many countries. Recently, however, a growing number of companies have started to ask a surprising question: what would happen if employees worked only four days a week but received the same salary?

Several large trials have tried to answer this question. In these programs, dozens of companies in different industries reduced working hours for six months or more. Researchers measured productivity, profits, and the wellbeing of staff before, during, and after the change.

The results were encouraging for supporters of the idea. Many companies reported that productivity stayed the same or even improved. Workers said they felt less stressed and more motivated. Fewer people took sick days, and fewer employees left their jobs to work somewhere else.

How is this possible? Part of the answer is that people waste a lot of time at work. Long meetings, constant emails, and unnecessary tasks fill the day. When teams have only four days, they are forced to focus on what really matters and cut activities that add little value.

The extra day off also gives people time to rest, exercise, care for family, and deal with personal tasks. As a result, they often return to work on Monday with more energy and better concentration. Some managers say their teams have become more creative.

Companies also discovered a hidden advantage in hiring. When a business offers a shorter week, it becomes far more attractive to job seekers, especially skilled young workers who value free time. Some small firms that could not compete with large employers on salary found that the four-day week helped them attract talented people.

Not every organization chose the same model. Some closed the whole office on Fridays, while others gave each employee a different day off so that customers could always reach someone. A few companies kept five days but shortened each working day. The best choice depended on the type of work and the needs of clients.

Still, the four-day week is not a perfect solution for everyone. It is much easier to introduce in an office than in a hospital, a school, or a factory that must stay open every day. Some workers also found that their four days became longer and more intense.

Experts suggest that companies should start with a careful trial, set clear goals, and listen to feedback from staff. The four-day week may not replace the traditional schedule everywhere, but it has started an important conversation about how, and how much, we should work.

title: Why Museums Are Going Digital
title_zh: 为什么博物馆正在走向数字化
author: Sophie Laurent
summary: Museums around the world are scanning their collections and building online exhibitions, which opens art and history to millions of new visitors.
paragraphs: For centuries, visiting a great museum meant traveling to a particular city, buying a ticket, and walking slowly through crowded halls. Today, a growing number of museums are offering another option. With a laptop or a phone, anyone can explore famous paintings, ancient tools, and rare manuscripts from home, often for free.

The process usually begins with digitization. Museum staff photograph objects in extremely high resolution, sometimes taking hundreds of images of a single item. For sculptures and other three-dimensional objects, they use special scanners to create detailed models that visitors can rotate on a screen and examine from every angle.

These digital collections have several advantages. Most museums can display only a small part of what they own, while the rest stays in storage rooms. Online, there is no shortage of wall space. Objects that have not been seen by the public for decades can suddenly be viewed by anyone with an internet connection.

Digital access is also valuable for education. Teachers can show students a historical document in close detail during a lesson. Researchers on the other side of the world can study an object without paying for an expensive trip. People with disabilities who find it difficult to visit in person can enjoy collections comfortably at home.

Some museums have become more creative. They offer virtual tours guided by curators, interactive timelines, and games that encourage young people to look closely at art. A few have invited the public to help, for example by reading and typing up old handwritten letters so that the texts become searchable.

The pandemic years sped up this trend dramatically. When buildings were forced to close, many institutions moved their programs online almost overnight. Some were surprised to find that their digital audience was far larger and more international than the visitors who normally came through their doors.

Of course, there are challenges. Digitizing a large collection is slow and expensive, and smaller museums often lack the money and technical skills. There are also questions about copyright, and about how to describe objects from other cultures respectfully, especially items that were taken during periods of colonial rule.

Few people believe that screens will replace real visits. Standing in front of an original painting, seeing its true size and texture, is a different experience. Instead, many curators see digital collections as an invitation. A person who discovers a painting online today may decide to travel and see it in person tomorrow.

title: Cooking at Home on a Busy Schedule
title_zh: 忙碌生活中如何在家做饭
author: Hannah Moore
summary: Cooking at home can save money and improve your diet, and a little planning makes it possible even when your week is extremely busy.
paragraphs: After a long day at work or school, ordering takeaway can feel like the only reasonable choice. Cooking seems to require time, energy, and skills that many of us simply do not have on a weekday evening. Yet people who cook at home regularly often say it saves money, improves their health, and even helps them relax.

The secret is usually planning rather than talent. Spending fifteen minutes on the weekend deciding what to eat during the week can remove a lot of stress. When you already know what you are going to cook, you are less likely to give up and reach for your phone to order food.

A shopping list based on your plan is the next step. Buying only what you need reduces waste and prevents those moments when you open the fridge and find nothing useful. It also helps to keep a few basic items at home, such as rice, pasta, eggs, canned beans, frozen vegetables, and a selection of spices.

Many busy cooks rely on a technique called batch cooking. On Sunday afternoon, they prepare large amounts of a few dishes, such as a vegetable soup, a pot of curry, or a tray of roasted chicken. These dishes are divided into containers and stored in the fridge or freezer, ready to be heated in minutes.

Another useful idea is to cook once and eat twice. If you are roasting vegetables for dinner, roast extra and add them to a salad or a wrap the next day. Leftover rice can become fried rice with a couple of eggs and some vegetables. This approach saves time without making meals boring.

Simple tools can make a real difference too. A sharp knife makes chopping faster and safer. A large frying pan, a good pot, and a rice cooker can handle most everyday meals. Some people find that a slow cooker is especially helpful, because they can add ingredients in the morning and come home to a hot meal.

It is important to be realistic. Nobody needs to cook a three-course dinner every night. A quick omelette with toast, a bowl of noodles with greens, or a sandwich with soup are all perfectly good meals. The goal is not to impress anyone but to eat reasonably well most of the time.

Finally, try to enjoy the process. Put on some music or a podcast, invite a friend or family member to help, and treat cooking as a break from screens. Over time, the skills grow naturally, and the kitchen can become one of the most relaxing places in your home.

title: The Hidden Energy Cost of Data Centers
title_zh: 数据中心隐藏的能源成本
author: Victor Alvarez
summary: Every search, stream, and AI request depends on data centers whose rapidly growing electricity and water consumption has become a pressing environmental concern.
paragraphs: Most of us think of the internet as something weightless, a cloud floating somewhere above our heads. In reality, every message we send, every film we stream, and every question we put to an artificial intelligence system is processed in an enormous, very physical building packed with servers, cables, and cooling equipment. These buildings are data centers, and their appetite for energy is growing rapidly.

Estimates vary, but data centers are widely believed to consume one to two percent of the world's electricity, a share comparable to that of some medium-sized countries. In regions where large technology companies have concentrated their facilities, the proportion can be dramatically higher, placing considerable strain on local power grids and occasionally delaying other construction projects.

The recent boom in artificial intelligence has intensified these concerns. Training a large language model requires thousands of specialized chips running continuously for weeks, and answering user requests afterwards demands substantial computing power as well. Analysts have warned that, unless efficiency improves substantially, demand from AI alone could rival the electricity consumption of entire nations within a decade.

Electricity is not the only resource involved. Servers generate a tremendous amount of heat, and keeping them within a safe temperature range often relies on water-based cooling systems. A single large facility can use millions of liters of water a day, which has provoked opposition in areas already suffering from drought.

The industry has responded in several ways. Engineers have designed more efficient chips and redesigned buildings so that cool outside air can be used whenever possible. Some operators have deliberately built facilities in cold climates such as northern Europe, while others are experimenting with liquid cooling, in which components are immersed directly in special fluids.

Major companies have also made ambitious commitments to power their operations with renewable energy. Critics, however, point out that buying renewable credits on paper is not the same as running a data center on clean power every hour of the day, particularly at night or when the wind is calm.

There is a more optimistic perspective as well. Digital services can replace activities that would otherwise consume far more energy, such as business travel or printing on paper. Furthermore, the efficiency of computing has improved remarkably for decades, which means that the energy needed for each individual calculation continues to fall.

Ultimately, the question is whether efficiency gains can keep pace with soaring demand. Achieving that balance will require transparent reporting by technology firms, sensible regulation, and perhaps a degree of restraint from users themselves. The cloud, it turns out, has a very real footprint on the ground.

title: The Economics of Free Shipping
title_zh: 免运费背后的经济学
author: Olivia Grant
summary: Free shipping is rarely free, and online retailers use it as a powerful psychological tool while quietly absorbing or redistributing its considerable costs.
paragraphs: Few phrases are as persuasive in online shopping as "free shipping." Countless studies have shown that unexpected delivery fees are among the most common reasons customers abandon their carts before completing a purchase. Consequently, retailers of every size have come under intense pressure to remove those fees, or at least to make them appear to disappear.

Of course, delivery is never genuinely free. Someone must pay for warehouses, packaging, fuel, drivers, and the notoriously expensive final stretch of the journey to a customer's door. The real question is how that cost is distributed, and the answers reveal a great deal about the psychology of consumers and the strategy of modern retail.

The simplest approach is to build the cost into product prices. A retailer might raise the price of an item slightly and then advertise delivery at no charge. Remarkably, many shoppers prefer this arrangement, even when the total is identical or higher, because a separate fee feels like a penalty, whereas a slightly higher price barely registers.

Another widespread tactic is the minimum order threshold. When delivery becomes free only above a certain amount, customers frequently add extra items to qualify. This behavior increases the average value of each order, which can more than compensate for the cost of shipping, since sending one larger parcel is cheaper than sending several small ones.

Membership programs take the idea further. By charging an annual fee in exchange for unlimited free delivery, a company converts shipping into a subscription. Members, having already paid, tend to concentrate their spending on that platform to get their money's worth, which strengthens customer loyalty and makes it harder for competitors to win them over.

For smaller businesses, however, competing with these giants can be painful. They lack the volume to negotiate discounts with carriers, and absorbing delivery costs may wipe out their already thin profit margins. Some have chosen to emphasize distinctive products and personal service instead, betting that loyal customers will accept a modest fee.

There are also environmental consequences. When shipping appears costless, consumers order more frequently, return items more casually, and choose faster delivery options that prevent efficient route planning. The result is more half-empty vans on the road and more cardboard in recycling bins, a burden that rarely appears on any receipt.

Free shipping, then, is best understood not as a gift but as a carefully engineered business decision. For shoppers, recognizing the hidden trade-offs can lead to more deliberate choices, such as combining orders or selecting slower delivery. For retailers, the challenge is to balance customer expectations against financial and environmental sustainability.

title: How Languages Borrow Words From Each Other
title_zh: 语言之间如何互相借用词汇
author: Thomas Whitfield
summary: Through trade, conquest, and technology, languages constantly absorb vocabulary from one another, and English offers an especially rich example of this process.
paragraphs: No language develops in complete isolation. Whenever communities come into contact through trade, migration, conquest, or cultural exchange, words begin to travel between them. Linguists call these travelers loanwords, and they offer a fascinating record of history, revealing who met whom, what they exchanged, and which ideas each society found worth naming.

English is an exceptionally enthusiastic borrower. After the Norman conquest of 1066, French became the language of the ruling class in England for several centuries, and thousands of French words entered everyday English. This is why English often possesses pairs of words with similar meanings, such as the native "ask" and the more formal, French-derived "inquire."

A memorable illustration involves food. The names of animals in the field, such as cow, pig, and sheep, come from Old English, the language of the farmers who raised them. The names of the meat served at the table, however, including beef, pork, and mutton, derive from French, reflecting the fact that the wealthy Norman elite were usually the ones eating it.

Later centuries brought further waves of borrowing. During the Renaissance, scholars introduced large numbers of Latin and Greek terms, particularly in science, medicine, and philosophy. As British trade and colonial power expanded, words arrived from every continent: "shampoo" and "pajamas" from India, "ketchup" probably from southern China, and "tycoon" from Japanese.

Borrowing is rarely a straightforward act of copying. Loanwords are typically adapted to the sound system of the receiving language, and their meanings frequently shift along the way. A word may become narrower, broader, or acquire an entirely new connotation, so that speakers of the original language might barely recognize it when they encounter it abroad.

The flow is by no means one-way. Today, English is the dominant source of new vocabulary for many languages, especially in technology, business, and popular culture. Terms such as "email," "weekend," and "online" appear in conversations from Tokyo to Berlin, sometimes provoking anxiety among those who fear their own language is being diluted.

Chinese provides an interesting contrast. Rather than simply imitating foreign sounds, Chinese often creates new words from existing characters that convey meaning. The word for computer, for instance, literally means "electric brain." Nevertheless, phonetic borrowings also exist, and some terms combine both strategies, capturing the sound and suggesting the sense at the same time.

Ultimately, borrowing demonstrates that languages are living systems rather than fixed monuments. Every loanword represents a moment of human contact, whether peaceful or violent, commercial or intellectual. For learners, recognizing these connections can make vocabulary far more memorable, transforming lists of words into stories about the people who first used them.

title: The Science of Building Lasting Habits
title_zh: 养成持久习惯的科学
author: Natalie Brennan
summary: Research suggests that lasting habits depend less on willpower than on cues, repetition, and environments deliberately designed to make good behavior easy.
paragraphs: Every January, millions of people resolve to exercise more, eat better, or read every night, and by February a large proportion have quietly abandoned their plans. The problem is rarely a lack of sincere intention. Rather, research in psychology suggests that most of us misunderstand how habits actually form and rely far too heavily on willpower, an unreliable resource at the best of times.

A habit is essentially a behavior that has become automatic through repetition in a consistent context. Psychologists often describe a loop consisting of three elements: a cue that triggers the behavior, the routine itself, and a reward that reinforces it. Over time, the brain links the cue directly to the routine, so that the action requires little conscious decision-making.

This explains why environment is so influential. People who keep a bowl of fruit on the kitchen counter tend to eat more fruit, while those who keep biscuits in view tend to snack on biscuits. Small changes in our surroundings can therefore have surprisingly large effects, because they alter the cues we encounter dozens of times each day.

One practical strategy is known as habit stacking, which involves attaching a new behavior to an existing one. For instance, someone might decide to do two minutes of stretching immediately after brushing their teeth every morning. Because the established routine already functions as a reliable cue, the new behavior has something stable to attach itself to.

It also helps to begin with goals that seem almost absurdly small. Committing to a single push-up or one page of reading may sound trivial, but it reduces resistance and allows the habit to take root. Once the behavior is automatic, it can gradually be expanded without the overwhelming feeling that so often leads people to quit.

Contrary to a widely repeated claim, there is no magic number of days required to form a habit. One frequently cited study found that the time needed ranged from about eighteen days to more than eight months, depending on the person and the complexity of the behavior. Encouragingly, missing an occasional day did not significantly disrupt the process.

Identity may matter as well. Some researchers argue that lasting change is more likely when people think of themselves in terms of who they want to become, such as "I am a runner," rather than focusing solely on outcomes like losing a certain amount of weight. Each small action then becomes evidence supporting that new self-image.

None of this means that change is effortless. However, the science offers a more forgiving and effective approach than simply trying harder. By designing supportive environments, starting small, and allowing time for repetition, ordinary people can build habits that last far beyond the first enthusiastic weeks of the year.

title: Learning to Code at Any Age
title_zh: 任何年龄都可以学编程
author: Kevin Walsh
summary: Learning to code is easier than many people think, and with free tools and a little practice every day, anyone can start.
paragraphs: Many people think that coding is only for young people or for math experts. This is not true. People of all ages learn to code, from children of eight to grandparents of seventy. Coding is a way to give instructions to a computer, and anyone who is patient can learn it.

Why should you learn to code? First, it can help you find a better job. Many companies need people who understand computers. Second, coding teaches you to solve problems step by step. Third, it is fun. You can make a small game, a simple website, or a tool that helps you every day.

Where should you start? A good first language is Python. It is easy to read because it looks a little like English. Another good choice is JavaScript, because it runs in every web browser. You do not need an expensive computer. An old laptop is enough for your first lessons.

There are many free ways to learn. Some websites teach coding with short videos and small tasks. You write a few lines of code and see the result right away. Many public libraries also have free classes. You can watch lessons online, too, and stop the video when you need more time.

Practice is the most important part. It is better to practice for twenty minutes every day than for five hours once a week. Your brain needs time to remember new ideas. Try to write a little code every day, even when you feel busy or tired.

You will make mistakes, and that is normal. Even expert programmers make mistakes every day. When your code does not work, the computer often shows an error message. Read it slowly. It usually tells you where the problem is. Fixing errors is a big part of learning.

It also helps to learn with other people. You can join an online group or a local club for new coders. You can ask questions and help others. When you explain an idea to someone else, you understand it better yourself. Friends also keep you going when learning feels hard.

Start with a small project that you care about. Maybe you want a program that tells you the weather or helps you plan your meals. Small wins give you confidence. Step by step, you will be surprised at how much you can do. It is never too late to begin.

title: How a Local Market Stays Busy
title_zh: 一个本地市场如何保持热闹
author: Maria Santos
summary: A small town market stays busy by offering fresh food, fair prices, and a friendly place where people enjoy meeting each other.
paragraphs: Every Saturday morning, the small town of Millbrook comes alive. In the main square, more than forty sellers open their tables at seven o'clock. They sell fruit, vegetables, bread, cheese, honey, and flowers. By nine o'clock, the square is full of people with shopping bags. The market has been open for more than fifty years.

Many towns have lost their old markets. Big supermarkets are often cheaper and open every day. So how does the Millbrook market stay so busy? The sellers and the town have worked together, and they have made a few smart choices over the years.

First, the food is very fresh. Most sellers are local farmers. They pick their fruit and vegetables on Friday and bring them to the market the next morning. Customers can taste the difference. A tomato from the market is often sweeter and softer than one from a big store.

Second, people can talk to the person who grew their food. They can ask how to cook a vegetable or when the strawberries will be ready. One farmer, Tom Harris, says that many of his customers have bought from him for twenty years. "They are not just customers," he says. "They are friends."

Third, the market is more than a place to shop. There is live music near the fountain, and children can paint pictures at a small table. Some sellers offer hot coffee and fresh pancakes. Families stay for hours. For many people, the market is the best part of their week.

The market has also changed with the times. Many sellers now accept card payments, not only cash. The market has a page online where sellers share news about their products. In winter, when there is less fruit, the town lets the market use a large hall so it can stay open.

Prices are fair, too. Some things cost a little more than in the supermarket, but many people are happy to pay. They know that their money helps local farmers and families. At the end of the day, sellers often sell extra fruit at a lower price, so nothing goes to waste.

The Millbrook market shows that small businesses can do well when they work together. Good food, friendly faces, and a nice place to meet are not easy to copy. As one customer said, "I can buy apples anywhere, but I come here for the people."

title: The Joy of Street Music
title_zh: 街头音乐的乐趣
author: Leo Fischer
summary: Street musicians bring music to busy cities, and their free performances make ordinary streets and stations more lively and friendly.
paragraphs: You walk through a busy train station on your way to work. Everyone is in a hurry. Then you hear a guitar and a beautiful voice. A young woman is singing near the stairs. Some people stop to listen. A child begins to dance. For a few minutes, the station feels like a different place.

Street music is one of the oldest kinds of music. For hundreds of years, musicians have played in streets, markets, and squares. In the past, they sang news and stories for people who could not read. Today, you can hear street music in almost every big city in the world.

People who play music in the street are often called buskers. Some buskers are students who want to practice in front of real people. Some are professional musicians who want to earn extra money. Others just love music and want to share it. They play guitar, violin, drums, piano, and many other instruments.

Buskers usually play for free. People who enjoy the music can put some money into an open guitar case or a hat. Today, many buskers also have a code that people can scan with their phones to pay. Some musicians also sell their own songs on small CDs or online.

Being a street musician is not always easy. The weather can be cold, wet, or very hot. Some people are not kind. In many cities, buskers need a permit to play in popular places. They may only play for one or two hours, and they must keep the music at a certain volume.

Still, street music can open doors. Some famous singers started their careers on the street. People filmed them with their phones, and the videos became popular online. A busker who plays in the same place every day can also become a well-known face in the neighborhood.

Many cities now see buskers as a good thing. Music makes streets feel safe and friendly. It brings people together, even if only for a moment. Some cities hold street music festivals, and some train stations even have a piano that anyone can play. People of all ages sit down and play.

Next time you hear music on the street, stop for a minute and listen. You do not have to give money, but a smile or a short clap means a lot. Street music is a small gift in a busy day, and it reminds us that art can be found anywhere.

title: My First Week Riding a Bike to Work
title_zh: 我骑车上班的第一周
author: Chris Taylor
summary: A writer describes the first week of riding a bike to work, including the hard moments and the surprising good changes that followed.
paragraphs: For five years, I drove my car to work every day. The trip was only six kilometers, but traffic was bad. I often sat in my car for thirty minutes and felt angry before my day even started. One evening, I looked at my old bike in the garage and decided to try something new.

On Monday morning, I was nervous. I checked the tires, put on a helmet, and packed my clothes in a small bag. The first few minutes felt strange. Cars passed me very closely, and I did not know the best way to go. I arrived at work hot and tired, but I was also proud of myself.

On Tuesday, my legs hurt a lot. Going up the hill near my office was very hard, and I had to stop and walk. A friend at work gave me some good advice. She said I should find a quieter road with a bike lane. That evening, I looked at a map and found a better way home.

The new road made Wednesday much better. It went through a park and along a small river. I saw ducks on the water and people walking their dogs. The trip took a few more minutes, but it was quiet and safe. For the first time, I really enjoyed the ride.

On Thursday, it rained. I almost took the car, but I put on a rain jacket and went anyway. It was not as bad as I thought. I was a little wet when I got to work, but I changed my clothes and felt fine. I also kept a towel in my desk after that.

By Friday, I noticed some changes. I slept better at night, and I felt more awake in the morning. I did not feel angry about traffic anymore. I also spent no money on fuel or parking that week. My colleagues asked me many questions, and two of them said they wanted to try it too.

Of course, riding a bike is not perfect for everyone. Some people live too far from work, and some jobs need a car. But if your trip is short, it may be worth a try. You do not need an expensive bike. You only need a safe road, a helmet, and a little courage.

It has now been three months, and I still ride my bike almost every day. My legs are stronger, and the hill is easy now. I leave the car at home for most trips. That first week was hard, but it changed my daily life in ways I did not expect.

title: Why Passwords Are Slowly Disappearing
title_zh: 为什么密码正在慢慢消失
author: Priya Desai
summary: Technology companies are replacing passwords with passkeys and other login methods that are both safer and easier for ordinary users.
paragraphs: For decades, the password has been the main key to our digital lives. We use passwords to open our email, check our bank accounts, and log in to countless websites. Yet most security experts agree that passwords are a weak and frustrating system, and the technology industry is now working hard to replace them.

The basic problem is human behavior. Strong passwords are long, random, and different for every account, which makes them almost impossible to remember. As a result, many people choose simple passwords or use the same one everywhere. When a single website is hacked, criminals try the stolen details on other popular services, often with success.

Passwords are also easy to steal through tricks. In a phishing attack, a criminal sends a message that looks like it comes from a real bank or company. The message leads to a fake website, and the victim types in their password without realizing it. Even careful users can be fooled by a convincing copy.

Over the past few years, extra protection has become common. Two-factor authentication asks users to confirm their identity with a second step, such as a code sent to their phone. This makes accounts much safer, but it also adds time and effort, and text message codes can still be intercepted by determined attackers.

The newest solution is called a passkey. Instead of a secret word, a passkey uses a pair of digital keys. One key is stored safely on your device, and the other is kept by the website. When you log in, your phone or computer proves that it has the right key, usually after you confirm with your fingerprint or face.

Passkeys have several important advantages. There is nothing to remember and nothing to type, so they cannot be guessed or reused. Because each passkey works only with the real website it was created for, phishing sites cannot trick you into handing it over. For most users, logging in becomes faster as well as safer.

The change will not happen overnight. Many websites still do not support passkeys, and some people worry about what will happen if they lose their phone. Companies are addressing this by allowing passkeys to be backed up and shared securely across devices, but the system can still feel confusing at first.

For now, the best advice is to use a password manager, turn on two-factor authentication, and try passkeys whenever a service offers them. One day, typing a password may seem as old-fashioned as sending a fax. Until then, a little care can keep your accounts much safer.

title: What Makes a Good Job Interview
title_zh: 怎样才算一次好的求职面试
author: James Okafor
summary: A successful job interview depends on careful preparation, clear examples from past experience, and thoughtful questions that show real interest in the role.
paragraphs: For many people, a job interview is one of the most stressful experiences in working life. In less than an hour, you have to convince a stranger that you are the right person for a position. The good news is that interviews follow fairly predictable patterns, and careful preparation can make a huge difference to the result.

The first step is research. Before the interview, read the job description carefully and visit the company's website. Try to understand what the company does, who its customers are, and what challenges it might be facing. Recruiters often say they are surprised by how many candidates know almost nothing about the organization.

Next, think about your own experience. Most interviewers ask questions about real situations, such as a time you solved a difficult problem or worked with a challenging colleague. A useful method is to describe the situation, the task, the action you took, and the result. Preparing four or five strong examples in advance will help you answer many different questions.

First impressions matter too. Arrive a little early, dress in a way that fits the company culture, and greet everyone politely, including the receptionist. In a video interview, check your camera and internet connection beforehand, choose a quiet room, and look at the camera rather than your own image on the screen.

During the interview, listen carefully to each question and take a moment to think before answering. It is perfectly acceptable to ask the interviewer to repeat or explain a question. Try to keep your answers focused and honest. If you do not know something, say so, and explain how you would find out.

Many candidates forget that an interview is a two-way conversation. Near the end, you will usually be invited to ask questions. This is a valuable opportunity. Asking about the team, the main goals for the first six months, or how success is measured shows that you are genuinely interested and thinking seriously about the role.

Body language also sends a message. Sitting up straight, making natural eye contact, and smiling occasionally help you appear confident and friendly. Nervousness is normal, and most interviewers expect it. Taking a slow breath before you answer can calm your voice and give you a little extra time to organize your thoughts.

Finally, follow up. A short email thanking the interviewer for their time is polite and keeps your name fresh in their mind. Whatever the outcome, every interview is a chance to learn. If you are not successful, ask for feedback when possible, and use it to prepare even better next time.

title: Why We Still Love Handwritten Letters
title_zh: 为什么我们仍然喜爱手写信
author: Grace Holloway
summary: In an age of instant messages, handwritten letters remain special because they take time, carry personality, and can be kept for many years.
paragraphs: Every day, billions of text messages and emails travel around the world in seconds. Communication has never been faster or cheaper. And yet, many people say that the most meaningful message they ever received was a letter written by hand. In a world full of screens, the simple handwritten letter seems to have kept a special kind of power.

Part of the reason is effort. Writing a letter takes time. You need paper, a pen, an envelope, and a stamp, and you have to think carefully about what you want to say, because it is difficult to delete a sentence. When someone receives a letter, they know that the writer chose to spend that time on them.

Handwriting also carries personality. Every person's writing is different. It may be neat or messy, large or small, careful or rushed. A letter from a grandparent, with its familiar shapes and small mistakes, feels personal in a way that typed words on a screen rarely do. Many people can recognize a friend's handwriting immediately.

Letters are physical objects, and that changes how we treat them. People keep old letters in boxes, drawers, and books for decades. They read them again on difficult days or share them with their children. Emails, by contrast, are often lost when we change phones or accounts, and few people ever print them out.

Historians are especially grateful for letters. Much of what we know about ordinary life in the past comes from letters between family members, soldiers and their loved ones, or friends living in different countries. Some experts worry that future historians will have far fewer personal documents to study, because digital messages are so easily deleted.

Interestingly, some young people are rediscovering letter writing. Pen pal websites connect strangers from different countries who want to exchange real letters. Shops that sell beautiful paper, stamps, and fountain pens report steady interest. On social media, people share photos of letters they have decorated with drawings, stickers, and dried flowers.

Teachers have noticed benefits too. Some research suggests that writing by hand helps people remember information better than typing. It forces the writer to slow down and choose words carefully. For language learners, writing a letter in a new language can be an excellent and enjoyable way to practice grammar and vocabulary.

Nobody expects handwritten letters to replace digital communication. Instant messages are practical, and they keep us connected every day. But perhaps that is exactly why letters feel so valuable. When almost everything is quick and easy, a slow and careful message reminds the reader that they are worth the extra effort.

title: How to Make Friends in a New City
title_zh: 如何在新城市交到朋友
author: Aisha Rahman
summary: Moving to a new city can feel lonely, but joining regular activities, saying yes to invitations, and being patient can help you build real friendships.
paragraphs: Moving to a new city can be exciting. There are new streets to explore, new restaurants to try, and new opportunities at work or university. But after the first few weeks, many people discover a less pleasant feeling: loneliness. Without old friends nearby, evenings and weekends can feel surprisingly empty. Fortunately, making friends as an adult is a skill that can be learned.

The first thing to understand is that friendships usually grow through repeated contact. Researchers have found that people need to spend many hours together before they become close friends. One meeting with a friendly stranger is rarely enough. That is why regular activities, where you see the same faces every week, are so helpful.

Think about what you already enjoy. If you like sports, join a local running club or a team that plays on weekends. If you prefer quieter hobbies, look for a book club, a language exchange, a choir, or a class in cooking or painting. Shared interests give you something easy to talk about, which removes a lot of pressure.

Volunteering is another excellent option. Helping at an animal shelter, a food bank, or a community garden allows you to meet kind people while doing something useful. Working side by side on a task often feels more natural than sitting across a table trying to think of conversation topics.

Your workplace or university can also be a good starting point. Accept invitations to lunch or after-work events, even if you feel a little tired or shy. Small moments, such as chatting in the kitchen or asking a colleague for advice about the city, can slowly turn into real friendships.

Technology can help, too. There are apps designed for meeting people who want friendship rather than romance, and many cities have online groups that organize walks, games, and meals. It may feel strange at first, but remember that the other people in these groups are usually looking for exactly the same thing as you.

Once you meet someone you like, take the next step. Suggest a coffee, a walk, or a visit to a market. Many people wait for others to make the first move, so being the one who invites can make a big difference. If they say no, do not take it personally. Try again another time, or with someone else.

Above all, be patient with yourself. Building a social life in a new place often takes six months to a year. Keep in touch with old friends while you make new ones, and notice small signs of progress, like a familiar face waving at you in the street. Little by little, the new city will start to feel like home.

title: Can Satellites Help Farmers Grow More Food?
title_zh: 卫星能帮助农民种出更多粮食吗？
author: Isabel Moreno
summary: Satellite imagery and data analysis are giving farmers detailed insight into crops and soil, though cost and connectivity still limit access for many smallholders.
paragraphs: Feeding a growing global population while using less water, fertilizer, and land is one of the defining challenges of this century. Increasingly, part of the solution is coming not from the field itself but from hundreds of kilometers above it. Satellites orbiting the Earth are now capturing information that allows farmers to monitor their crops with a precision that was unimaginable a generation ago.

The principle is straightforward. Healthy plants reflect light in distinctive ways, particularly in the near-infrared range, which is invisible to the human eye. By measuring how much light of different wavelengths a field reflects, satellite sensors can estimate how vigorously crops are growing and identify areas where they may be suffering from drought, disease, or a shortage of nutrients.

Several public programs, notably the European Sentinel satellites and the American Landsat series, make such images freely available. A single location may be photographed every few days, enabling farmers and agronomists to follow the development of a crop throughout the season and to detect problems long before they would be visible from the ground.

This information becomes particularly powerful when combined with other data. Weather records, soil samples, and measurements from sensors on tractors can be integrated into software that generates detailed maps. These maps allow a farmer to apply fertilizer or water only where it is genuinely needed, an approach known as precision agriculture, which reduces costs and limits environmental damage.

Satellites also contribute to planning on a much larger scale. Governments and international organizations use them to forecast harvests, anticipate food shortages, and target assistance before a crisis becomes a famine. Insurance companies increasingly rely on satellite data to verify crop losses quickly, enabling compensation to reach affected farmers without lengthy inspections.

Nevertheless, significant obstacles remain. Interpreting raw imagery requires expertise, and many commercial services that translate data into practical advice are expensive. Smallholder farmers, who produce a substantial proportion of the world's food, often lack reliable internet connections, and their fields may be smaller than the resolution of freely available images can accurately capture.

Cloud cover presents an additional difficulty, since optical sensors cannot see through it. Radar satellites, which can observe the ground regardless of weather or daylight, partially address this limitation, but their data are considerably more complex to analyze. Researchers are therefore training machine learning models to combine multiple sources and fill in the gaps automatically.

Encouragingly, initiatives are emerging that deliver simplified recommendations by text message in local languages, bringing the benefits of satellite monitoring to farmers with only basic phones. If such efforts can be expanded affordably, the view from space may prove to be one of the most valuable tools available for securing a sustainable food supply.

title: Why Supply Chains Became Front-Page News
title_zh: 为什么供应链成了头条新闻
author: Benjamin Hartley
summary: Recent disruptions revealed how fragile global supply chains had become, prompting companies to reconsider efficiency, resilience, and where their products are made.
paragraphs: Until recently, few consumers gave much thought to supply chains, the complex networks of suppliers, factories, ports, and transport companies that move products from raw materials to store shelves. These systems functioned so smoothly that they were practically invisible. Then, in the space of a few years, a series of disruptions turned them into a subject of daily headlines and kitchen-table conversations.

The pandemic was the most dramatic trigger. Factories closed temporarily, workers fell ill, and demand shifted abruptly as people stopped spending on travel and started buying home office equipment, exercise bikes, and electronics. Shipping containers ended up in the wrong places, ports became congested, and the cost of moving goods across oceans rose to extraordinary levels.

Other shocks followed. A single enormous container ship became stuck in the Suez Canal for six days, blocking one of the world's busiest trade routes. Shortages of semiconductors forced car manufacturers to halt production lines, while extreme weather and geopolitical conflicts interrupted the supply of energy, grain, and fertilizer.

These events exposed a vulnerability that had developed over decades. In pursuit of efficiency, many companies had embraced so-called just-in-time production, keeping minimal inventory and relying on parts arriving precisely when needed. They had also concentrated manufacturing in a small number of low-cost locations. This model minimized expenses in normal times but left little margin for error.

In response, businesses have begun to prioritize resilience alongside cost. Some are holding larger stocks of critical components, accepting higher storage expenses as a form of insurance. Others are diversifying their suppliers across several countries, a strategy sometimes described as "China plus one," so that a problem in a single region does not halt production entirely.

A related trend is nearshoring, in which companies move production closer to their main markets. American firms have expanded operations in Mexico, for instance, while European manufacturers have looked toward Eastern Europe and North Africa. Governments have reinforced this shift with subsidies designed to bring strategically important industries, particularly chip manufacturing, back within their borders.

Technology is also playing a role. Advanced software now allows companies to track shipments in real time, model the effects of potential disruptions, and identify hidden dependencies several layers down the chain. Many firms discovered during the crisis that they had no idea who supplied their suppliers, and they are now investing heavily to gain that visibility.

None of these adjustments is free, and consumers may ultimately bear part of the cost through higher prices. Yet the experience of recent years has convinced many executives that the cheapest supply chain is not necessarily the best. The new objective is a system efficient enough to remain competitive and robust enough to withstand the next unexpected shock.

title: The Quiet Revival of Board Games
title_zh: 桌游的悄然复兴
author: Fiona MacLeod
summary: Despite the dominance of digital entertainment, board games have enjoyed a remarkable revival, driven by inventive design, crowdfunding, and a desire for face-to-face connection.
paragraphs: In an era dominated by smartphones and streaming services, one might have predicted that board games would gradually fade into nostalgic obscurity. Instead, the opposite has occurred. Over the past two decades, the tabletop game industry has expanded considerably, board game cafes have opened in cities across the world, and thousands of new titles are published every year.

Part of this revival stems from a transformation in design. Many traditional family games relied heavily on luck, with players rolling dice and moving pieces according to chance, while one participant might be eliminated long before the end. Modern designers, influenced strongly by a wave of German games in the nineties, have emphasized strategy, meaningful decisions, and mechanisms that keep everyone involved until the final turn.

The variety available today is remarkable. Cooperative games require players to work together against the game itself, for example by containing the spread of diseases or escaping a sinking island. Others involve negotiation, deduction, or the construction of elaborate civilizations over several hours. Simpler party games, meanwhile, can be learned in minutes and suit large, lively groups.

Crowdfunding platforms have played a significant role. Independent designers can now present a concept directly to potential players and raise money before production begins, bypassing traditional publishers. Some campaigns have raised millions of dollars, although the model also carries risks, since backers occasionally wait years for delayed products or receive games that fall short of their expectations.

Perhaps the most important factor, however, is social. Board games offer a rare opportunity to sit face to face with friends or family, free from the constant interruptions of notifications. Many enthusiasts describe a game night as a structured excuse to spend time together, providing shared goals and conversation while removing the awkwardness of simply meeting to talk.

Ironically, digital technology has also fueled the trend. Online videos explain complicated rules clearly, reducing the barrier for newcomers, while popular channels review games and showcase lively matches. Companion apps can manage scoring or narrate stories, and digital versions allow friends separated by distance to continue playing together.

Researchers and educators have noticed potential benefits as well. Games can encourage planning, probability reasoning, and negotiation skills, and some schools use them to teach subjects ranging from history to economics. Studies involving older adults suggest that regular play may help maintain cognitive function, although further research is needed to establish firm conclusions.

The board game revival therefore reflects more than a passing fashion. It suggests that, amid abundant digital entertainment, many people still crave tangible objects, shared physical spaces, and the unpredictable laughter that arises when friends gather around a table. The humble cardboard box, it seems, continues to hold a surprising amount of joy.

title: Why Boredom Might Be Good for You
title_zh: 为什么无聊可能对你有好处
author: Owen Gallagher
summary: Psychologists increasingly argue that occasional boredom is a valuable signal that encourages creativity, reflection, and the pursuit of more meaningful goals.
paragraphs: Few experiences are as universally disliked as boredom. Waiting in a queue, sitting through a tedious meeting, or facing an empty afternoon with nothing to do can feel almost unbearable. Today, of course, relief is always within reach: a smartphone offers an endless stream of messages, videos, and news. Yet a growing body of research suggests that by eliminating boredom so efficiently, we may be losing something valuable.

Psychologists generally define boredom as the uncomfortable feeling of wanting to engage in satisfying activity but being unable to do so. Crucially, it functions as a signal. Much like hunger tells us to eat, boredom indicates that our current situation is failing to meet our needs and motivates us to search for something more stimulating or meaningful.

One of the most frequently cited benefits concerns creativity. In a well-known experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately dull task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently generated more inventive ideas in a creative challenge than those who had not been bored. Researchers suspect that boredom encourages the mind to wander, allowing unusual connections to form.

This wandering state is associated with what neuroscientists call the default mode network, a set of brain regions that becomes active when we are not focused on an external task. Activity in this network appears to support daydreaming, autobiographical memory, and imagining the future, processes that help us make sense of our experiences and plan our lives.

Boredom may also prompt valuable reflection. When we are not constantly occupied, we are more likely to ask whether our work, relationships, and routines are genuinely fulfilling. In this sense, boredom can serve as a catalyst for change, pushing people to learn new skills, pursue different careers, or reconsider priorities they had previously taken for granted.

Constant digital stimulation, however, can prevent this process from unfolding. Many people now reach for their phones at the first hint of boredom, filling every spare moment with information. Some researchers argue that this habit may weaken our ability to tolerate quiet moments and could even make ordinary activities feel more boring by comparison.

It is important to distinguish occasional boredom from chronic boredom, which has been linked to anxiety, depression, and risky behavior. The aim is not to seek out endless monotony but to allow brief, unstructured periods in which the mind is free to drift. Short walks without headphones or a few minutes gazing out of a window can be sufficient.

Parents and teachers might take particular note. Children who are permitted to experience boredom often invent games, stories, and projects of their own. Rather than rushing to fill every empty moment, we might treat boredom as an invitation, an opportunity to discover what we genuinely want to do next.
